case.case_title: Sasanasiritissa Thero and Others v. P.A. De Silva, Chief Inspector, C.I.D. and Others
case.source_citation: Sri Lanka Law Reports (1989) 2 Sri LR 356

clause.text: Any person detained shall be brought before a judge and cannot be held without legal order.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the petitioners' detention without being produced before a Magistrate and continued detention under Emergency Regulations violated Article 13(2).
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioners claimed they were detained without being brought before a judge and without valid legal orders, violating Article 13(2).
case_context.respondent_argument: Respondents argued detention was lawful under Emergency Regulations, supported by detention orders under Regulation 17(1) and 19(2).
key_facts: Petitioners were detained for 73 days under Regulation 19(2) without being produced before a Magistrate.
On 01.01.88, petitioners were served with a detention order dated 20.12.87 under Regulation 17(1).
Petitioners were not informed of earlier detention orders and were not produced before a Magistrate.
The detention orders were signed by the Secretary and Additional Secretaries of the Ministry of Defence.
The petitioners challenged the legality and mala fides of the detention orders.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The Court held that detention without production before a Magistrate was permissible under the Emergency Regulations but must be supported by valid detention orders. The entire detention period from 20.12.87 was treated as a single detention. The Court emphasized the necessity of good faith in issuing detention orders and found mala fides in the issuance of the impugned detention order.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The Court found the petitioners were not produced before a Magistrate, but this was consistent with Emergency Regulations. However, the detention orders, especially the one dated 20.12.87, were issued mala fide without credible material, rendering the detention unlawful under Article 13(2).
principles_established: Detention under Emergency Regulations does not require production before a Magistrate.
Detention must be supported by valid detention orders issued in good faith.
Mala fide issuance of detention orders violates Article 13(2).
The entire period of detention under successive orders can be treated as a single detention for relief purposes.

outcome.holding: The Court held that the petitioners' detention violated Article 13(2) due to mala fide issuance of detention orders and ordered compensation for unlawful detention.
outcome.remedy_or_orders: Declaration that the detention is unlawful; compensation awarded to petitioners.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 13(2) was central to the Court's finding that the petitioners' prolonged detention without lawful and bona fide detention orders violated their fundamental rights, leading to relief.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: Petitioners were detained without being produced before a Magistrate; detention orders were issued under Emergency Regulations but were found mala fide and unsupported by credible material, rendering detention unlawful.
